Name: Apple01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Apple01_Description", "A small, palm-sized fruit with smooth skin that blushes deep red over pale yellow. Wild apples were gathered by humans for at least 750,000 years before domestication began around 4000 BCE in the mountains of Kazakhstan. The seeds within contain trace amounts of cyanide - a defense mechanism that ironically helped spread the species as animals discarded bitter seeds far from parent trees.")

Name: Berries01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Berries01_Description", "A handful of small, dark berries gathered from thorny bushes. Berry-gathering was a cornerstone of Paleolithic nutrition - high in sugars and vitamins that were otherwise scarce. Learning to distinguish edible berries from poisonous lookalikes was essential knowledge passed down through countless generations.")

Name: EdibleRoot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "EdibleRoot01_Description", "A starchy tuber dug from the earth with a digging stick. Underground storage organs were crucial to human survival - they store concentrated calories year-round when fruits and game are scarce. The earliest digging sticks, simple pointed branches, predate even stone tools. Some researchers argue that tuber exploitation drove human brain evolution.")

Name: Mushroom01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Mushroom01_Description", "A fleshy fungus growing from decaying wood. Mushroom identification is among the most dangerous foraging knowledge - deadly species often closely resemble edible ones. Yet fungi provided essential nutrients and possibly medicine to ancient peoples. Some researchers believe Otzi the Iceman carried medicinal fungi 5,300 years ago.")

Name: Nuts01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Nuts01_Description", "Hard-shelled nuts gathered from hazel bushes. Nuts were a critical calorie source for Paleolithic peoples - high in fat and protein, they store well through winter when other foods are scarce. Archaeological sites across Europe contain massive deposits of hazelnut shells, suggesting organized autumn harvesting and storage.")

Name: Acorns01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Acorns01_Description", "The nuts of oak trees, rich in starch but bitter with tannins. Raw acorns are unpalatable and can cause digestive distress. However, with proper processing - repeated leaching in water - they become a nutritious staple. Acorn processing required understanding of chemistry that developed over generations.")

Name: BirdEgg01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BirdEgg01_Description", "A speckled egg taken from a ground nest. Eggs were among the earliest protein sources exploited by our ancestors - requiring only discovery, not hunting. The shells themselves had value: ostrich eggshells were used as water containers and beads in Africa over 60,000 years ago.")

Name: Stick01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Stick01_Description", "A freshly-cut branch still supple with sap. Green wood bends without breaking, essential for making bows, basket rims, and tool handles. The moisture content must be carefully managed - too wet and it warps as it dries; too dry and it snaps. Understanding wood seasoning was crucial knowledge.")

Name: FallenBranch01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FallenBranch01_Description", "A dry branch found on the forest floor. Dead wood served countless purposes - fuel for fires, shafts for spears, clubs for defense. The oldest wooden artifacts ever found, the 400,000-year-old Schöningen spears, were crafted from branches of the slow-growing spruce tree, selected for their straight grain.")

Name: StraightBranch01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "StraightBranch01_Description", "A remarkably straight branch, rare in nature and highly valued. Straight shafts were essential for spears, arrows, and atlatl darts - a crooked shaft flies erratically. Ancient hunters spent considerable effort seeking, selecting, and straightening wooden shafts, sometimes using heat and pressure to correct natural curves.")

Name: Bark01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Bark01_Description", "A sheet of bark peeled from a tree trunk. Bark served multiple purposes across human history - the outer layer burns readily for fire-starting, while the inner bast layer contains strong fibers for cordage. Birch bark was especially prized for its waterproof properties, used for canoes, roofing, and containers.")

Name: PlantFiber01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "PlantFiber01_Description", "Long, flexible fibers extracted from plant stems or bark. The oldest known cordage - found at Abri du Maras in France - dates to at least 50,000 years ago, made by Neanderthals. The technology of twisting fibers was a cognitive breakthrough enabling nets, snares, hafted tools, and eventually textiles.")

Name: RiverCobble01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "RiverCobble01_Description", "A smooth, rounded stone worn by river currents over millennia. River cobbles were humanitys first tools - used without modification for pounding, grinding, and throwing. The selection of the right cobble - proper weight, comfortable grip, suitable hardness - was the first step toward tool-making that would define our species.")

Name: FlintNodule01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FlintNodule01_Description", "A nodule of flint with its characteristic waxy luster visible where the chalky cortex has chipped. Flint is cryptocrystalline silica formed in chalk deposits from the remains of ancient sea sponges. Its conchoidal fracture produces edges sharper than surgical steel - a property our ancestors exploited for over two million years.")

Name: ChertNodule01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "ChertNodule01_Description", "A nodule of chert, a siliceous rock similar to flint but formed in different geological conditions. While not as fine-grained as true flint, chert still fractures predictably and was widely used where flint was unavailable. Many archaeological sites far from chalk deposits contain tools made from local chert sources.")

Name: QuartziteCobble01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "QuartziteCobble01_Description", "A hard cobble of metamorphosed sandstone. Quartzite was among the first materials worked by our earliest ancestors - the 2.6 million-year-old Oldowan tools from Gona, Ethiopia include quartzite choppers. While its fracture is less predictable than flint, quartzite is found in many regions where finer stones are absent.")

Name: Hammerstone01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Hammerstone01_Description", "A carefully selected cobble that fits naturally in the palm, with good weight for striking. For over two million years, hammerstones were the primary tool-making tool - used to strike flakes from stone cores. The wear patterns on archaeological hammerstones reveal they were used for thousands of strikes before being discarded.")

Name: OldowanChopper01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "OldowanChopper01_Description", "A cobble with flakes removed from one end to create a crude cutting edge - the defining tool of the Oldowan industry, humanitys first recognizable technology. For over a million years, from 2.6 to 1.7 million years ago, choppers like this were the height of technological achievement. Studies show they produce about three inches of cutting edge per pound of stone.")

Name: SharpFlake01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SharpFlake01_Description", "A thin fragment of stone with a razor-sharp edge, struck from a larger core. These simple flakes - technically waste products of tool-making - were among humanitys first cutting tools. Oldowan toolmakers 2.6 million years ago discovered that even crude flakes could slice through hide and sinew more efficiently than teeth or fingernails.")

Name: SimpleScraper01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SimpleScraper01_Description", "A stone flake carefully retouched along one edge to create a steep, sturdy scraping surface. Scrapers were among the first specialized tools - Oldowan knappers recognized that different edge angles suited different tasks. The steep scraping edge removes material without cutting through, perfect for cleaning hides or shaping wood.")

Name: DiggingStick01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DiggingStick01_Description", "A hardwood stick with one end sharpened to a point. The digging stick is arguably humanitys oldest tool - even simpler than stone implements. Chimpanzees use similar tools to extract termites, suggesting this technology predates our species. For humans, digging sticks unlocked the calories stored in underground tubers and roots.")

Name: CrudeClub01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CrudeClub01_Description", "A heavy branch selected for use as a weapon. The club is perhaps the simplest weapon - requiring no modification beyond selection of an appropriate branch. Even chimpanzees use branches as clubs in dominance displays. For early humans, clubs served for both hunting and defense against predators and rivals.")
ShortDescription: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CrudeClub01_ShortDescription", "A heavy branch used as a club.")

Name: ThrowingStone01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "ThrowingStone01_Description", "A smooth, palm-sized stone selected for throwing. Humans are uniquely adapted for throwing - our shoulder structure, wrist flexibility, and hand proportions evolved specifically for this purpose. The ability to throw stones accurately allowed early humans to hunt and defend themselves at a distance, a crucial advantage.")

Name: Cordage01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Cordage01_Description", "Plant fibers twisted into a two-ply cord. The technique is deceptively complex: fibers are first twisted in one direction, then two strands are twisted together in the opposite direction. This opposing twist locks the fibers in tension, creating strength far exceeding the individual strands. Cordage enabled snares, hafting, and countless other technologies.")

Name: RawMeat01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "RawMeat01_Description", "Fresh meat from a hunted animal. Before the control of fire, our ancestors consumed meat raw - a practice that continued alongside cooking for efficiency. Raw meat carries risks of parasites and bacteria, but provides essential proteins, fats, and nutrients. The ability to process meat with stone tools was a defining human adaptation.")

Name: Bone01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Bone01_Description", "A bone salvaged from a butchered animal. Bones were never wasted by our ancestors - they served as raw material for tools, containers for marrow fat, and fuel for fires in treeless regions. The working of bone into needles, awls, and harpoons represented a technological leap beyond stone alone.")

Name: Sinew01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Sinew01_Description", "Tough, fibrous tendon stripped from an animal carcass. Sinew was the strongest cordage material available to prehistoric peoples - stronger than any plant fiber. When dried, it shrinks and hardens, making it ideal for hafting tools and backing bows. Properly processed sinew remains strong for centuries.")

Name: AnimalHide01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "AnimalHide01_Description", "The fresh skin of an animal, still bearing traces of fat and flesh. Raw hide must be processed quickly before it rots - a race against decay that shaped early human behavior. The transformation of putrescible skin into durable leather was a crucial technology for survival in cold climates, enabling clothing and shelter.")

Name: DryTinder01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DryTinder01_Description", "Fine, dry material that catches sparks readily - shredded bark, dried grass, or fungal amadou. Fire-starting requires understanding the ignition hierarchy: tinder catches sparks, kindling sustains the small flame, and fuel maintains the fire. Without proper tinder, even the best fire-starting technique fails.")

Name: Firewood01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Firewood01_Description", "Dry wood suitable for burning. Not all wood burns equally - resinous softwoods ignite easily but burn fast, while dense hardwoods require more heat but last longer. Seasoned (dried) wood burns cleaner than green wood. Understanding fuel selection was essential knowledge for maintaining fires through cold nights.")

Name: HandDrillSpindle01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "HandDrillSpindle01_Description", "A straight, dry stick shaped for friction fire-making. The hand drill is the most basic friction fire method - the spindle is rotated rapidly between the palms while pressing down onto a fireboard. This technique requires enormous stamina and callused hands, but needs no tools beyond the spindle and board.")

Name: Fireboard01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Fireboard01_Description", "A flat piece of dry, soft wood with a notch cut for collecting hot dust. The fireboard is half of the friction fire system - the spindle rotates in a depression on the board, generating friction heat. The notch allows hot dust to accumulate until it reaches ignition temperature. Wood selection is critical: cottonwood, willow, and cedar work well.")

Name: TinderBundle01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "TinderBundle01_Description", "A carefully constructed nest of fine, dry material designed to catch an ember and burst into flame when blown upon. The tinder bundle represents accumulated knowledge - which materials ignite easiest, how to arrange them for airflow, and the breathing technique needed to coax ember to flame without smothering it.")
ShortDescription: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "TinderBundle01_ShortDescription", "A prepared bundle for catching embers.")

Name: HandAxe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "HandAxe01_Description", "A teardrop-shaped stone tool flaked on both faces to create a symmetrical cutting edge - the hallmark of Acheulean technology. These elegant tools appeared 1.7 million years ago and remained virtually unchanged for over a million years, the longest-lasting tool design in human history. The bifacial technique produces twelve inches of cutting edge per pound of stone.")

Name: FlintKnife01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FlintKnife01_Description", "A flint blade carefully retouched along one edge to create a durable cutting tool while leaving the opposite edge blunt for safe handling. The conchoidal fracture of flint produces an edge only a few molecules thick - sharper than modern surgical steel. Such knives remained the pinnacle of cutting technology until bronze working.")

Name: AntlerTine01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "AntlerTine01_Description", "A pointed tine from a deer or elk antler. Antler was prized by prehistoric peoples for its unique properties - hard yet slightly flexible, it could be shaped by soaking and carving. Antler tines served as pressure flakers for fine stone work, punches, handles, and eventually harpoon points.")

Name: PressureFlaker01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "PressureFlaker01_Description", "An antler tine shaped for precision stone working. Unlike percussion flaking which strikes flakes loose, pressure flaking uses steady force to push tiny flakes from a stone edge. This technique, developed in the Upper Paleolithic, enabled the creation of delicate points and blades impossible to achieve with hammerstones alone.")
ShortDescription: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "PressureFlaker01_ShortDescription", "An antler tool for fine flaking.")

Name: BoneAwl01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BoneAwl01_Description", "A bone splinter ground to a sharp point for piercing holes in leather and bark. Awls were essential for creating sewn clothing, which enabled human expansion into cold climates. The oldest known eyed needles appear around 25,000 years ago, but simpler awls predate them by tens of thousands of years.")

Name: WoodenSpear01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WoodenSpear01_Description", "A straight branch sharpened to a point. The oldest known spears - from Schöningen, Germany - are 400,000 years old, crafted with remarkable sophistication for their time. The point was carved to center the weight for throwing, and the wood was carefully selected for its straight grain. Simple but effective.")

Name: FireHardenedSpear01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FireHardenedSpear01_Description", "A wooden spear with its tip hardened by controlled exposure to fire. Heat treatment drives out moisture and partially carbonizes the wood fibers, creating a harder, more durable point. The Schöningen spears show evidence of this technique 400,000 years ago - fire was a tool as much as a comfort.")

Name: CookedMeat01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CookedMeat01_Description", "Meat cooked over an open fire until browned and aromatic. The control of fire - perhaps 400,000 years ago - transformed human nutrition. Cooking denatures proteins, kills parasites, and effectively pre-digests food. Some researchers argue that cooking freed metabolic energy for brain development, enabling the cognitive leaps that followed.")

Name: RoastedRoot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "RoastedRoot01_Description", "A starchy tuber roasted in the coals of a fire until soft and sweet. Cooking transforms raw starches into more digestible forms, dramatically increasing caloric availability. Archaeological evidence suggests that cooking roots was among the earliest uses of fire, predating the roasting of meat in some regions.")

Name: SmokedMeat01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SmokedMeat01_Description", "Meat preserved through extended exposure to smoke. Smoking was one of humanitys earliest preservation methods - the phenols and aldehydes in smoke inhibit bacterial growth while partially dehydrating the meat. Properly smoked meat can last months, enabling food storage that smoothed the boom-bust cycle of hunting.")

Name: ScrapedHide01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "ScrapedHide01_Description", "An animal hide with the flesh and fat carefully scraped away using stone scrapers. This intermediate stage of hide processing must be completed before the skin rots. The scraping removes tissue that would decay while leaving the collagen fiber matrix intact. Proper fleshing is essential - any remaining fat will eventually spoil.")

Name: SmokeTannedLeather01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SmokeTannedLeather01_Description", "Leather preserved through extended smoking after scraping and softening. Smoke tanning is among the oldest preservation methods - the phenolic compounds in smoke bond with collagen fibers, preventing decay and adding water resistance. This simple technique produces durable leather suitable for clothing and containers.")

Name: SimplePouch01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SimplePouch01_Description", "A small bag made from a single piece of leather, gathered and tied with sinew cord. Containers revolutionized human life - enabling the transport of water, gathered foods, and tools. Before pottery, leather and woven containers were essential for any mobility beyond immediate consumption.")

Name: BowDrillKit01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BowDrillKit01_Description", "A complete friction fire set: bow, spindle, fireboard, and handhold. The bow drill multiplied the efficiency of friction fire-making - the cord wrapped around the spindle converts the back-and-forth sawing motion into rapid rotation. This mechanical advantage made fire-starting accessible to more people, not just those with exceptional hand strength and calluses.")
ShortDescription: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BowDrillKit01_ShortDescription", "A complete bow drill fire kit.")

Name: BoneNeedle01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BoneNeedle01_Description", "A slender bone splinter with an eye drilled through one end for threading. The eyed needle, appearing around 25,000 BCE, revolutionized clothing construction. Before needles, garments were limited to simple wraps and ties. With needles, fitted clothing became possible - sewn boots, tailored parkas, and layered garments that enabled human survival in the Arctic.")

Name: Atlatl01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Atlatl01_Description", "A carved wooden throwing stick with a hook or spur at one end to engage the butt of a dart. The atlatl - appearing around 30,000 BCE - was humanitys first true weapon multiplier. By effectively lengthening the arm, it doubles throwing velocity and triples effective range. Atlatl-thrown darts could bring down mammoths from safe distances.")

Name: AtlatlDart01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "AtlatlDart01_Description", "A fletched projectile designed for use with an atlatl. Unlike spears, atlatl darts are flexible shafts that store and release energy during the throw - the flex amplifies the power transfer. The rear end has a concave socket that engages the atlatl hook, while stone points and fletching ensure accurate, lethal flight.")

Name: SimpleBow01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SimpleBow01_Description", "A curved stave of springy wood with a cord stretched between its ends. The bow appeared independently on every inhabited continent - a testament to its elegant simplicity. By storing muscle energy in bent wood and releasing it instantly, the bow launches projectiles faster than any arm could throw. Early bows were self-bows: single staves of yew, ash, or osage orange.")

Name: StoneArrow01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "StoneArrow01_Description", "A slender wooden shaft with a knapped stone point and feather fletching. Arrow-making is a complex craft - the shaft must be straight, the point properly sized and hafted, the fletching aligned to impart stabilizing spin. Each arrow represents hours of skilled work, yet might be lost or broken in a single shot.")
ShortDescription: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "StoneArrow01_ShortDescription", "A fletched arrow with stone point.")

Name: FishingSpear01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FishingSpear01_Description", "A multi-pronged spear designed for taking fish in shallow water. Unlike hunting spears with single points, fishing spears have barbed tines that trap slippery prey. The earliest fishing spears used fire-hardened wooden prongs; later versions incorporated bone or stone barbs. Spearfishing requires understanding light refraction - fish are not where they appear.")

Name: BoneHook01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BoneHook01_Description", "A curved hook carved from bone with a sharp point for catching fish. Fish hooks appeared at least 23,000 years ago in East Timor. The gorge hook - a straight sliver that catches sideways in the throat - predates the curved hook. Early anglers used plant fiber lines, baiting hooks with insects, worms, or bits of fish to attract prey.")

Name: FishNet01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FishNet01_Description", "A mesh of knotted plant fiber designed to trap fish in water. Net-making represents a significant investment - hours of cordage production and careful knotting. But a well-made net can catch dozens of fish at once, transforming the economics of subsistence. The oldest known fishing net fragments date to around 8300 BCE in Finland.")

Name: FishTrap01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FishTrap01_Description", "A woven basket trap that guides fish into an enclosure from which they cannot escape. Fish traps work passively - once set in a stream or tidal area, they continue catching fish without attention. The design exploits fish behavior: swimming into constricting funnels but unable to find the exit. Such traps were used worldwide for millennia.")

Name: RawFish01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "RawFish01_Description", "A freshly caught fish, still glistening wet. Fish were a crucial protein source for coastal and riverine peoples. Unlike mammals, fish can be eaten raw with lower parasite risk (though not zero). The omega-3 fatty acids in fish may have contributed to human brain development as coastal populations exploited this resource.")

Name: CookedFish01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CookedFish01_Description", "A fish cooked over open flame until the flesh flakes easily. Cooking fish destroys parasites and makes the protein more digestible, but the greatest advantage may be preservation - smoked and dried fish can be stored for months. Archaeological fish bones at coastal sites reveal that fishing was a dietary staple by the Upper Paleolithic.")

Name: DriedFish01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DriedFish01_Description", "Fish preserved through air-drying and smoking. Drying removes the moisture bacteria need to cause decay, creating food that lasts months or years. In Arctic regions, peoples learned to freeze-dry fish in winter winds. In warmer climates, smoking added antibacterial compounds. Dried fish was a trade good across prehistoric Europe and Asia.")

Name: Microlith01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Microlith01_Description", "A tiny geometric blade designed to be hafted in combination with others. Microliths emerged in the late Paleolithic as a brilliant innovation - instead of one large point, many small blades set in a row create a serrated cutting edge. When one microlith breaks, only it needs replacement, not the whole tool. This modular approach revolutionized tool design.")

Name: MicrolithSickle01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "MicrolithSickle01_Description", "A curved wooden or bone handle set with a row of microliths to create a serrated cutting edge. The microlith sickle was essential for harvesting wild grasses - precursor to the agricultural sickle. Wear patterns called sickle gloss form on the microliths from cutting silica-rich grass stems, revealing these tools purposes across millennia.")

Name: BrainTannedLeather01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BrainTannedLeather01_Description", "Supple leather processed by working animal brain oils into the hide. The old saying every animal has enough brains to tan its own hide is nearly true - brain tissue contains phospholipids that lubricate collagen fibers, preventing them from bonding stiff. Brain-tanned leather is soft, breathable, and can be washed, unlike bark-tanned leather.")

Name: LeatherTunic01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "LeatherTunic01_Description", "A simple garment of stitched leather that covers the torso. The development of sewn clothing, enabled by bone needles, transformed human adaptation to cold climates. A leather tunic provides protection from wind, sun, and abrasion while allowing full range of motion. Such garments enabled human expansion into environments previously impossible to survive.")

Name: LeatherTrousers01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "LeatherTrousers01_Description", "Leg coverings of stitched leather, essential for travel through brush and cold weather. Archaeological evidence suggests fitted leg garments developed in Eurasia, possibly in response to horse riding. The 5,300-year-old clothing of Otzi the Iceman included goat-leather leggings, showing the ancient lineage of this practical garment.")

Name: LeatherBoots01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "LeatherBoots01_Description", "Foot coverings of thick leather with sewn soles. Footwear fundamentally changed human mobility - protecting feet from rocks, thorns, cold, and hot sand. The oldest known leather shoe, found in Armenia, dates to 5,500 years ago. Earlier footwear likely included simple moccasins and sandals that left no archaeological trace.")

Name: HarpoonHead01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "HarpoonHead01_Description", "A barbed point carved from bone or antler, designed to detach from its shaft while remaining connected by a line. The toggling harpoon was a breakthrough in marine hunting - when the point penetrates, it twists sideways and cannot be pulled out. This allowed humans to hunt seals, walrus, and even whales that would otherwise escape.")

Name: DugoutCanoe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DugoutCanoe01_Description", "A watercraft hollowed from a single log using fire and stone tools. The dugout canoe was humanitys first true vessel, enabling river travel, coastal fishing, and island colonization. The oldest known example dates to around 8000 BCE in the Netherlands. Creating a dugout required weeks of careful work - charring the interior and scraping out the carbon with stone adzes.")
ShortDescription: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DugoutCanoe01_ShortDescription", "A canoe carved from a log.")

Name: Paddle01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Paddle01_Description", "A carved wooden blade attached to a handle for propelling watercraft. The paddle is an extension of the human arm into water - its broad surface pushes water backward to drive a boat forward. Early paddles were single-piece, carved from split logs. The design has remained essentially unchanged for millennia because physics demands certain proportions.")

Name: GroundStoneAxe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "GroundStoneAxe01_Description", "A stone axe head shaped by grinding rather than flaking. Ground stone technology, emerging in the Mesolithic, produced tougher tools than flaked stone - essential for heavy woodworking. The grinding process takes hours but creates a smooth surface that cuts more efficiently and resists chipping. Such axes made dugout canoes and timber construction possible.")

Name: HaftedAxe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "HaftedAxe01_Description", "A ground stone axe head mounted in a wooden handle using rawhide or plant fiber bindings. Hafting multiplied the power of stone tools - the handle acts as a lever, allowing powerful swings impossible with handheld stones. This innovation made felling trees practical, enabling deforestation for agriculture and construction of timber structures.")
ShortDescription: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "HaftedAxe01_ShortDescription", "A stone axe with wooden handle.")

Name: Adze01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Adze01_Description", "A woodworking tool with the blade set perpendicular to the handle, used for shaping timber with a swinging, chopping motion. While axes cut across the grain, adzes shave along it - essential for hollowing canoes and smoothing planks. The adze was the primary woodworking tool before the development of metal planes.")

Name: WovenBasket01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WovenBasket01_Description", "A container made from interlaced plant materials - reeds, willow, or bark strips. Basket weaving is among humanitys oldest crafts, predating pottery by thousands of years. Unlike pottery, baskets are lightweight and resilient, ideal for gathering and transport. The techniques - coiling, plaiting, twining - require only natural materials and skilled hands.")

Name: WaterSkin01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WaterSkin01_Description", "A container made from a complete animal stomach or bladder, used to carry water. Before pottery, water transport depended on organic containers. Animal bladders and stomachs, naturally waterproof, required only cleaning and a closure. Such containers enabled travel through waterless terrain - a crucial adaptation for human expansion.")

Name: BarkContainer01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BarkContainer01_Description", "A vessel fashioned from a single piece of flexible bark, folded and sewn or pegged together. Birch bark was especially prized - waterproof, flexible when fresh, and light. Northern peoples used bark containers for everything from berry collection to cooking (water in a tight bark vessel can be boiled by adding hot stones).")

Name: CompositeBow01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CompositeBow01_Description", "A bow made from multiple materials laminated together - wood, horn, and sinew. The composite bow stores more energy in less space than a simple self-bow, producing tremendous power from a short weapon. Developed on the steppes of Central Asia, composite bows could be used from horseback and shoot farther than any self-bow. Construction requires months of skilled work and curing.")

Name: SinewBackedBow01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SinewBackedBow01_Description", "A wooden bow reinforced with a layer of sinew on its back (the side facing away from the archer). Sinew under tension is stronger than wood - adding it to the bows back prevents breakage and stores additional energy. This intermediate technology bridge between simple and composite bows spread wherever suitable wood was scarce.")

Name: FletchedArrow01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FletchedArrow01_Description", "An arrow with carefully applied feather fletching that imparts stabilizing spin during flight. The three-feather configuration, set at an angle, causes rotation that keeps the arrow point-forward - the same principle as rifling in firearms. Proper fletching dramatically improves accuracy and range over unfletched shafts.")

Name: Quiver01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Quiver01_Description", "A container designed to hold and protect arrows while allowing quick access. Quivers are made from leather, bark, or woven materials, often decorated to display status. The design varies by culture - back quivers for hunting, hip quivers for war, ground quivers for siege. A good quiver protects fletching while keeping arrows ready.")

Name: SnareWire01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SnareWire01_Description", "A trap made from cordage, designed to tighten around an animals leg or neck as it passes through. Snares are passive hunters - once set, they work without human presence. This efficiency made snaring essential for subsistence hunting, allowing one person to maintain dozens of traps while engaging in other activities.")

Name: Deadfall01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Deadfall01_Description", "A trap that drops a heavy weight on an animal when triggered. The figure-four trigger is an ingenious mechanism - three sticks notched to interlock under tension, collapsing when disturbed. Deadfalls kill instantly without damaging pelts, and can take animals too large for snares. The design dates back thousands of years.")

Name: CrudePottery01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CrudePottery01_Description", "A hand-formed clay vessel, dried and fired in an open fire. The earliest pottery, appearing around 20,000 BCE in East Asia, was shaped without a wheel - coiled from ropes of clay or pinched from a single lump. Open-fire pottery reaches lower temperatures than kiln-fired ware, producing porous vessels suitable for storage and simple cooking.")

Name: CookingPot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CookingPot01_Description", "A ceramic vessel designed for cooking over fire. Pottery revolutionized cooking - clay vessels can hold liquids at boiling temperatures indefinitely, enabling stews, soups, and porridges impossible to make in skin or bark containers. The thick walls retain heat, allowing slow cooking that breaks down tough fibers and extracts nutrients from bones.")

Name: StorageJar01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "StorageJar01_Description", "A large ceramic vessel for storing grain, oil, or other goods. Food storage transformed human society - surplus production became possible, enabling specialization and social complexity. Clay jars protected contents from pests and moisture, allowing grain storage through winter or lean years. The development of storage pottery marks a key step toward agricultural civilization.")

Name: ClayBowl01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "ClayBowl01_Description", "A shallow ceramic vessel for serving and eating food. Bowls are among the simplest pottery forms - a pinched or coiled shape dried and fired. Before pottery, eating involved sharing a single cooking vessel or placing food on leaves. Individual bowls changed the social dynamics of eating and enabled portion control.")

Name: DiggingHoe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DiggingHoe01_Description", "A stone blade hafted perpendicular to a wooden handle, used for breaking and turning soil. The hoe was the first agricultural implement - transforming wild soil into cultivated ground. Before the plow, all farming was done with hoes and digging sticks. This backbreaking tool fed civilizations for millennia and is still used worldwide.")

Name: PlantingStick01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "PlantingStick01_Description", "A pointed stick used to create holes for planting seeds. The planting stick - also called a dibble - is agriculture reduced to its essence. A human making holes in dirt and dropping in seeds. This simple tool enabled the Neolithic Revolution, the transition from foraging to farming that changed human destiny.")

Name: GrainStore01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "GrainStore01_Description", "Seeds from wild grasses, gathered for food. Long before cultivation, humans gathered wild grains - wheat, barley, and rice ancestors grew wild across Eurasia. The grains required processing to be edible: threshing to remove husks, winnowing to separate chaff, and grinding or cooking. This labor-intensive food source became worthwhile when game grew scarce.")

Name: GrindingStone01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "GrindingStone01_Description", "A pair of stones - a large flat base and a smaller handheld mano - used to grind grain into flour. Grinding stones (metates and manos) were essential technology for grain-eating peoples worldwide. The repetitive motion wore distinctive grooves in the stone and in the bodies of those who used them - archaeological skeletons show wear patterns from hours of daily grinding.")

Name: FlatBread01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FlatBread01_Description", "A simple bread made from ground grain mixed with water and cooked on a hot stone. Flatbreads were humanitys first baked goods - requiring only grain, water, and heat. Unleavened flatbreads like tortillas, chapati, and matzoh remain staples worldwide. The transformation of indigestible raw grain into nourishing bread was a cornerstone of civilization.")

Name: Porridge01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Porridge01_Description", "Cracked or ground grain boiled into a thick mush. Porridge requires less grinding than bread and no baking, making it an efficient way to eat grain. Hot porridge warms the body, delivers calories, and can incorporate other foods. Archaeological residues show porridge was eaten across the ancient world from Scotland to China.")

Name: SpinningWhorl01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SpinningWhorl01_Description", "A weighted disk that adds momentum to a drop spindle for spinning fiber into thread. The spindle whorl was among humanitys most important inventions - transforming loose fibers into continuous thread. Before the spinning wheel, all thread was spun on hand spindles. A skilled spinner could produce remarkable quantities of fine thread with this simple tool.")

Name: LinenThread01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "LinenThread01_Description", "Thread spun from flax plant fibers. Flax was among the first plants cultivated for fiber rather than food. Linen thread is strong, smooth, and takes dye well. The process of creating linen - retting, breaking, scutching, hackling, and spinning - was a lengthy process mastered by Neolithic peoples who valued cloth highly.")

Name: WoolThread01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WoolThread01_Description", "Thread spun from sheep fleece. Sheep were domesticated around 10,000 BCE, but woolly sheep - bred for fiber rather than meat - appeared much later. Wool has remarkable properties: it insulates when wet, resists fire, and takes dye beautifully. Wool spinning requires different techniques than plant fibers due to the scales on each fiber.")

Name: WovenCloth01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WovenCloth01_Description", "Fabric created by interlacing warp and weft threads on a loom. Woven cloth required enormous labor - growing or gathering fiber, processing it, spinning thread, and weaving on a loom. This investment made cloth precious in the ancient world, often serving as currency. The development of weaving enabled clothing that draped, fitted, and decorated the human form.")

Name: SimpleLoom01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SimpleLoom01_Description", "A portable loom tensioned by a strap around the weavers body. The backstrap loom was humanitys first true weaving device - simpler than frame looms but capable of producing complex patterns. The weaver controls tension with their own body, creating an intimate connection between maker and cloth. Such looms are still used worldwide.")

Name: ClothTunic01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "ClothTunic01_Description", "A garment of woven fabric cut and sewn to cover the torso. Cloth tunics were cooler than leather in warm weather, easier to clean, and could display colors and patterns. The simple T-shaped tunic, requiring minimal cutting and sewing, was the basic garment across ancient civilizations from Egypt to China.")

Name: NativeCopper01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "NativeCopper01_Description", "Naturally occurring pure copper, found in nugget form. Native copper was humanitys first metal - it could be worked without smelting, simply hammered cold or heated to soften. Deposits in the Great Lakes region, Cyprus, and elsewhere were exploited for millennia. Native copper objects predate true metallurgy by thousands of years.")

Name: CopperAwl01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CopperAwl01_Description", "A pointed tool hammered from native copper. Copper awls were among the first metal tools - stronger than bone, they could pierce tough materials without breaking. The bright color and permanence of copper made even simple tools prestige items. Such awls marked the beginning of the metal ages.")

Name: CopperBead01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CopperBead01_Description", "A small ornament hammered from native copper. Copper beads were among humanitys first metal objects - beautiful, permanent, and signifying status. The malleability of copper allowed hammering into complex shapes impossible with stone. Such ornaments were traded across vast distances in prehistoric exchange networks.")

Name: BarkTannedLeather01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BarkTannedLeather01_Description", "Leather preserved using tannins extracted from tree bark. Bark tanning produces stiff, water-resistant leather ideal for soles, scabbards, and armor. The process takes months - hides soaked in increasingly strong bark solutions until the tannins fully penetrate. This chemistry was discovered independently worldwide wherever oaks and similar trees grew.")

Name: LeatherArmor01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "LeatherArmor01_Description", "Protective body covering made from multiple layers of hardened leather. Leather armor offers reasonable protection with lighter weight than metal. Boiled or waxed leather (cuir bouilli) becomes rigid enough to deflect glancing blows. Such armor equipped warriors from ancient times through the Middle Ages.")

Name: WoodenShield01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WoodenShield01_Description", "A defensive implement of wood, often faced with leather. Shields transformed combat - allowing defense without retreating. Wooden shields could be made quickly from available materials. Rawhide facing added resilience, while the wooden core absorbed impacts. Shield designs varied by culture but all served to protect the warrior.")

Name: OilLamp01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "OilLamp01_Description", "A clay vessel holding oil with a wick for producing light. Oil lamps provided controlled, portable illumination inside dwellings. The earliest lamps used animal fat; later versions burned plant oils. A simple lamp could burn for hours, extending productive time into darkness. This humble technology enabled work, worship, and socializing after sunset.")

Name: CopperOre01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CopperOre01_Description", "Rock containing copper minerals, typically malachite or azurite. Recognizing ore required knowledge - the green and blue staining that indicates copper presence. Mining ore was harder than finding native copper but far more abundant. The discovery that heat could extract metal from rock launched true metallurgy.")

Name: TinOre01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "TinOre01_Description", "Rock containing cassiterite, the primary tin mineral. Tin deposits are rare and unevenly distributed, making tin a strategic resource. Ancient peoples discovered that adding tin to copper produced bronze - harder and more durable than either metal alone. This discovery sparked the Bronze Age and drove long-distance trade.")

Name: Charcoal01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Charcoal01_Description", "Wood converted to nearly pure carbon by burning in limited oxygen. Charcoal burns hotter than wood and with less smoke - essential for metalworking. The charcoal burner was a vital tradesperson, maintaining smoldering piles for days to produce this crucial fuel. Without charcoal, metal smelting would be impossible.")

Name: Bellows01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Bellows01_Description", "A device for forcing air into a fire to increase temperature. Bellows enabled the high temperatures needed for metal smelting - human lungs alone cannot sustain the airflow required. The simple bag bellows, squeezed by hand, was the first type. Later developments included foot-operated bellows that freed both hands for smithing.")

Name: SmeltingCrucible01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SmeltingCrucible01_Description", "A heat-resistant vessel for melting metal. Crucibles enabled controlled metalworking - melting ore or scrap to pour into molds. Made from clay mixed with sand or ground pottery, crucibles could withstand repeated heating. Archaeological crucibles show slag residues that reveal the metals worked and techniques used.")

Name: BronzeIngot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeIngot01_Description", "A standardized block of bronze alloy - copper mixed with tin. Bronze revolutionized human technology - harder than pure copper, it held sharper edges and resisted deformation. The typical ratio was about 90% copper to 10% tin. Bronze ingots were traded across the ancient world as currency and raw material.")

Name: BronzeKnife01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeKnife01_Description", "A knife blade cast from bronze, the first truly durable metal cutting tool. Bronze knives could be sharpened repeatedly, surviving far longer than stone blades. The casting process allowed mass production - identical knives from the same mold. Such standardization was impossible with hand-knapped stone.")

Name: BronzeAxe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeAxe01_Description", "An axe head cast from bronze, far superior to stone for woodworking. Bronze axes transformed forestry and construction - felling trees in fraction of the time required with stone tools. The socketed axe head, cast with a hole for the handle, was a Bronze Age innovation that created a stronger tool.")

Name: BronzeSword01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeSword01_Description", "A sword blade cast from bronze - humanitys first true sword. Before bronze, swords were impossible - stone and copper lacked the strength for long blades. Bronze swords could be cast in one piece, ground sharp, and maintained through campaigns. They transformed warfare from the skirmish to the pitched battle.")

Name: BronzeSpearhead01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeSpearhead01_Description", "A leaf-shaped spear point cast from bronze. Bronze spearheads brought metal warfare to the masses - simpler and cheaper to produce than swords, spears armed common infantry. The socketed design allowed quick replacement of broken shafts. Thousands of bronze spearheads have been recovered from ancient battlefields.")

Name: BronzeArrowhead01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeArrowhead01_Description", "An arrowhead cast from bronze, deadlier than stone points. Bronze arrowheads could be mass-produced in molds, standardizing ammunition. They penetrated armor better than stone and caused more severe wounds. The transition to bronze arrowheads marked the professionalization of warfare.")

Name: BronzeHelmet01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeHelmet01_Description", "Head protection formed from bronze sheet or cast in sections. Bronze helmets offered unprecedented protection for warriors. The metal could be shaped to deflect blows and fitted with crests and plumes for visibility and intimidation. Such helmets marked their wearers as elite fighters.")

Name: BronzeShield01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeShield01_Description", "A defensive shield faced with bronze sheet. Bronze shields were lighter than solid wood while offering superior protection. The metal facing could be decorated with embossed designs - lions, eagles, or geometric patterns that identified the warrior. Such shields were prestige items, often buried with their owners.")

Name: PottersWheel01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "PottersWheel01_Description", "A rotating platform for shaping clay symmetrically. The potters wheel revolutionized ceramic production - enabling faster production and more consistent shapes. Wheel-thrown pottery has characteristic marks: concentric rings inside, smooth curves outside. This innovation, developed around 3500 BCE, remained the standard for millennia.")

Name: WheelThrownPot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WheelThrownPot01_Description", "A ceramic vessel shaped on a potters wheel. Wheel-thrown pottery is thinner, lighter, and more uniform than hand-built ware. The spinning motion creates naturally symmetrical forms. Such pottery could be produced faster than hand-building, enabling specialized potters who made wares for trade.")

Name: Chariot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Chariot01_Description", "A light, two-wheeled vehicle drawn by horses, carrying a driver and warrior. The chariot transformed Bronze Age warfare - its speed and mobility dominated battlefields from Egypt to China. Building a chariot required specialized skills: wheelwrighting, woodworking, leatherworking, and metalworking combined. Chariots were weapons of the elite.")

Name: SpokedWheel01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SpokedWheel01_Description", "A wheel with a hub, spokes, and rim - lighter and stronger than solid wheels. The spoked wheel enabled fast chariots and carts. Creating proper spokes required understanding of wood grain and stress distribution. This engineering achievement spread rapidly across the ancient world, remaining the standard wheel design until modern times.")

Name: ScaleArmor01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "ScaleArmor01_Description", "Body armor made from overlapping bronze scales sewn to a leather backing. Scale armor provided flexible protection - the overlapping plates deflected blows while allowing movement. Such armor required thousands of individual scales, making it expensive. Scale armor protected elite warriors from archers and light infantry.")

Name: BronzeGreaves01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeGreaves01_Description", "Shin guards formed from bronze, protecting the lower legs. Greaves were essential protection for infantry - the lower legs were vulnerable targets in close combat. Properly fitted greaves covered from knee to ankle, often lined with leather or cloth for comfort. Archaeological finds show greaves were sometimes decorated with faces or animals.")

Name: GlazedPottery01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "GlazedPottery01_Description", "Ceramic ware coated with a glassy surface. Glazing made pottery waterproof and easier to clean. The technique required specific mineral additions and carefully controlled firing. Glazed vessels could hold liquids without seepage and displayed brilliant colors. This technology enabled specialized containers for oils, wines, and medicines.")

Name: GlassBeads01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "GlassBeads01_Description", "Small decorative objects made from molten sand. Glass-making emerged in Bronze Age Mesopotamia and Egypt, producing beads that imitated precious stones. The technology required high temperatures and knowledge of specific mineral additions. Glass beads became valuable trade items, found in graves far from their origins.")

Name: BronzeSaw01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeSaw01_Description", "A toothed metal blade for cutting wood. Bronze saws enabled precise woodworking impossible with stone tools - straight cuts, uniform boards, and detailed joinery. The teeth had to be individually filed and set. Saws transformed furniture-making and construction, enabling fitted joints and smooth surfaces.")

Name: BronzeChisel01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeChisel01_Description", "A metal tool for carving wood and stone. Bronze chisels held edges better than copper and far outlasted stone tools. They enabled detailed carving - decorative reliefs, fitted joints, and inscriptions. The chisel and mallet became symbols of the craftsman, essential tools for builders and artists alike.")

Name: WritingTablet01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WritingTablet01_Description", "A flat piece of clay for recording information with a stylus. Clay tablets were the first widespread writing medium. Cuneiform script pressed into wet clay recorded everything from royal decrees to beer rations. When dried or fired, tablets became permanent records. Tens of thousands survive, revealing the ancient world.")

Name: Stylus01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Stylus01_Description", "A pointed implement for impressing marks into soft clay. The reed stylus, cut at an angle, created the wedge-shaped marks of cuneiform writing. Scribes trained for years to master the hundreds of signs. The stylus was the tool of administrators and priests who controlled information.")

Name: IronOre01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronOre01_Description", "Rock containing iron minerals, typically hematite or magnetite. Iron is far more common than copper or tin, but requires higher temperatures to smelt. The discovery of iron working around 1200 BCE transformed civilization - abundant iron made metal tools available to common people, not just elites.")

Name: IronBloom01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronBloom01_Description", "A spongy mass of iron mixed with slag, produced by smelting ore. Unlike bronze, which can be cast, early iron had to be worked solid - the bloom was heated and hammered repeatedly to expel slag and consolidate the metal. This laborious process required skill and stamina, but produced workable iron.")

Name: WroughtIron01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WroughtIron01_Description", "Iron that has been forged to remove impurities and create a workable bar. Wrought iron is relatively soft but extremely tough - it bends rather than breaks. The forging process aligns the iron grains, creating strength. Such bars were the standard form for trade and storage of iron.")

Name: IronKnife01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronKnife01_Description", "A knife blade forged from iron. Iron knives were harder than bronze, held edges longer, and could be resharpened many times. As iron became common, every household could afford metal knives. This democratization of metal tools transformed daily life from cooking to crafting.")

Name: IronAxe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronAxe01_Description", "An axe head forged from iron. Iron axes cut faster than bronze and were cheaper to produce once iron-working was established. They enabled rapid deforestation for agriculture and construction. The abundance of iron tools transformed landscapes across Eurasia and Africa.")

Name: IronSword01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronSword01_Description", "A sword blade forged from iron. Iron swords could be made longer than bronze without becoming brittle. They reshaped warfare - iron equipped larger armies as the metal became affordable. The quality varied enormously, from soft wrought iron to early steels that approached modern performance.")

Name: IronSpearhead01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronSpearhead01_Description", "A spear point forged from iron. Iron spearheads equipped the mass armies of the ancient world - from Greek hoplites to Roman legions. The ubiquity of iron made metal weapons standard rather than elite. A village blacksmith could produce spearheads, arming local militias.")

Name: SteelIngot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SteelIngot01_Description", "Iron with controlled carbon content, harder and springier than pure iron. Steel - iron with added carbon - was discovered when iron was heated in charcoal. The carbon diffuses into the surface, creating a harder material. True steel-making required understanding of quenching and tempering, knowledge that developed gradually.")

Name: SteelSword01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SteelSword01_Description", "A sword of hardened steel, superior to both bronze and iron. Steel swords could hold razor edges and spring back from bends that would permanently deform iron. Such weapons were prized possessions, often named and passed down through generations. The best steel swords became legendary.")

Name: ChainMail01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "ChainMail01_Description", "Armor made from interlocking metal rings. Chain mail provided flexible protection that moved with the body. Creating mail required thousands of individual rings, each linked to four neighbors. The labor was enormous, but the result protected against slashing weapons while allowing full movement.")

Name: IronHelmet01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronHelmet01_Description", "Head protection forged from iron. Iron helmets could be made thicker and stronger than bronze, providing better protection. Designs varied by culture - from simple bowls to elaborate crested helms. Iron helmets equipped common soldiers as iron became affordable.")

Name: IronShield01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronShield01_Description", "A wooden shield reinforced with iron fittings. Iron rims and bosses strengthened shields that would otherwise split from sword blows. The central iron boss protected the grip and could be used offensively. Such shields equipped the warriors of late antiquity.")

Name: PlowShare01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "PlowShare01_Description", "The cutting blade of a plow, forged from iron. Iron plowshares cut through heavy soils that defeated wooden plows, opening new lands to agriculture. The moldboard plow, with its iron share, enabled farming of northern Europes clay soils. This tool fed the medieval world.")

Name: IronNails01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronNails01_Description", "Small iron fasteners for joining wood. Nails transformed construction - enabling faster assembly than joinery and stronger joints than wooden pegs. A blacksmith could produce hundreds of nails per day. Nails were valuable enough to be salvaged from burning buildings in frontier areas.")

Name: Horseshoe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Horseshoe01_Description", "A curved iron plate nailed to a horses hoof for protection. Horseshoes enabled horses to work on hard roads and rocky terrain without wearing their hooves. The technology spread in the early medieval period, transforming transportation and warfare by keeping horses sound through hard use.")

Name: Anvil01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Anvil01_Description", "A heavy iron block on which metal is shaped by hammering. The anvil is the essential tool of the blacksmith - its mass provides resistance for forging, while its shaped surfaces enable specific forming operations. A good anvil could last generations, becoming a family heirloom.")

Name: Tongs01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Tongs01_Description", "Iron tools for gripping hot metal. Tongs enabled the smith to manipulate red-hot iron safely and precisely. Different shapes suited different work - flat jaws for bar stock, round for rods, specialized forms for specific tasks. Tongs were often the first tools a new smith made.")

Name: SmithHammer01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SmithHammer01_Description", "A heavy iron hammer designed for metalworking. The smiths hammer shapes metal through thousands of precise blows. Different weights and face shapes suited different work - heavy hammers for drawing out, light hammers for finishing. The hammer became the symbol of the smith and of industry itself.")

Name: Stone01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Stone01_Description", "A common stone suitable for throwing or simple tasks. Humans have selected and used natural stones for over 3 million years - the first tools required no modification at all, just recognition of a useful shape.")

Name: Flint01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Flint01_Description", "High-quality flint nodule with the conchoidal fracture pattern essential for knapping. Flint was so valuable in prehistory that it was traded hundreds of miles from its sources. The best flint comes from chalk deposits where silica replaced ancient sea creatures.")

Name: Branch01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Branch01_Description", "A fallen branch suitable for various uses. Gathering deadfall was safer than cutting live wood and provided already-seasoned material. Different tree species offered different properties - willow for flexibility, oak for strength.")

Name: Hardwood01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Hardwood01_Description", "Dense hardwood from oak, ash, or similar species. Hardwoods grow slowly, packing more cellulose into each growth ring. This density made them essential for tool handles, weapon hafts, and anything requiring strength and durability.")

Name: Softwood01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Softwood01_Description", "Light softwood from pine, spruce, or similar conifers. Softwoods grow quickly and work easily with stone tools. Their lower density made them ideal for friction fire hearths, floats, and situations where weight mattered.")

Name: LargeLog01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "LargeLog01_Description", "A substantial log requiring significant effort to harvest with stone tools. Felling large trees was a major undertaking before metal axes - fire-girdling (burning a ring around the trunk) was often used to kill trees before cutting.")

Name: Plank01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Plank01_Description", "A split wooden plank. Before saws, planks were produced by splitting logs along the grain using wooden wedges. This technique, called riving, produced stronger planks than sawing because it followed natural wood fibers.")

Name: BowStave01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BowStave01_Description", "A carefully selected and seasoned piece of wood suitable for bow-making. The best bow staves come from the boundary between heartwood and sapwood, combining the compression strength of heartwood with the tension strength of sapwood.")

Name: ArrowShaft01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "ArrowShaft01_Description", "A straight wooden shaft suitable for arrow-making. Arrow shafts required careful selection - they needed to be straight, properly dried, and matched in weight and spine (flexibility) for consistent flight.")

Name: Clay01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Clay01_Description", "Workable clay gathered from riverbanks or deposits. Clay particles are so fine they hold water between them, allowing the material to be shaped. Different clays fire to different colors - iron-rich clay becomes red, clean clay fires white.")

Name: Sand01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Sand01_Description", "Fine sand useful for pottery tempering, grinding, and glass-making. Not all sand works for all purposes - beach sand contains salt that causes problems, while river sand is often ideal for construction.")

Name: Sandstone01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Sandstone01_Description", "Sandstone with abrasive surface ideal for grinding and shaping. Natural sandstone served as humanity\'s first grinding tools - the grit embedded in the stone wore away other materials through friction.")

Name: Greenstone01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Greenstone01_Description", "Dense greenstone (jade, nephrite, or serpentine) prized for ground stone tools. These metamorphic rocks are extremely tough and take a fine polish. Greenstone axes were so valuable they were often more ceremonial than practical.")

Name: Resin01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Resin01_Description", "Sticky tree resin collected from pine or birch wounds. Resin was prehistory\'s superglue - it could be softened by heating, applied, and hardened to create waterproof, durable bonds. Birch tar required sophisticated pyrolysis to produce.")

Name: BirchBark01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BirchBark01_Description", "Flexible birch bark peeled in sheets. Birch bark is naturally waterproof and rot-resistant due to its oils. It served as roofing, containers, and even writing material across the northern hemisphere for millennia.")

Name: OakBark01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "OakBark01_Description", "Oak bark rich in tannins for leather processing. The tannins in oak bark bind to animal hide proteins, transforming soft putrescible skin into durable leather. This discovery revolutionized clothing and equipment.")

Name: DriedGrass01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DriedGrass01_Description", "Bundles of dried grass for tinder, bedding, and cordage. Grass was humanity\'s most versatile plant material - it could be twisted into rope, woven into mats, or used as insulation. Dried grass catches sparks easily for fire-starting.")

Name: Reeds01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Reeds01_Description", "Tall reeds from wetland areas. Reeds provided straight, hollow stems useful for arrow shafts, blow tubes, and weaving. Reed boats, made by bundling stems together, may have carried the first ocean voyagers.")

Name: FlaxFiber01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FlaxFiber01_Description", "Processed flax fibers ready for spinning. Flax was among the first domesticated fiber plants, cultivated by 8000 BCE. Its long, strong fibers produce linen - a fabric that becomes softer with washing and can last for centuries.")

Name: WoolFleece01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "WoolFleece01_Description", "Raw wool sheared from sheep. Wool was a revolutionary fiber - unlike plant fibers, it insulates even when wet. Early sheep had hair, not wool; selective breeding over millennia produced the fluffy fleeces we know today.")

Name: Feathers01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Feathers01_Description", "Bird feathers suitable for arrow fletching. Fletching stabilizes arrow flight through drag - the feathers catch air and prevent tumbling. Fletchers learned to use feathers from the same wing to create consistent spin.")

Name: Horn01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Horn01_Description", "Animal horn from cattle, goats, or sheep. Horn is keratin - the same protein as fingernails - and can be softened with heat and shaped. Horn containers, combs, and tool handles were common across all pastoral cultures.")

Name: AnimalBrain01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "AnimalBrain01_Description", "Fresh animal brain for hide tanning. Brain-tanning uses the lecithin in brain tissue to soften leather. Remarkably, every animal has roughly enough brain to tan its own hide - a fact known to tanners for millennia.")

Name: AnimalBladder01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "AnimalBladder01_Description", "Cleaned animal bladder for containers. Bladders provided waterproof, flexible containers before pottery. They could hold water, oil, or even be inflated as floats. Nothing was wasted from a successful hunt.")

Name: HideGlue01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "HideGlue01_Description", "Adhesive made by boiling hide scraps. Collagen in animal skin breaks down into gelatin when boiled - this gelatin dries into a strong, reversible adhesive. Hide glue remains superior to synthetic glues for some applications today.")

Name: Water01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Water01_Description", "Clean water essential for countless processes. Access to clean water shaped human settlement patterns throughout prehistory. Water was needed for drinking, cooking, pottery, tanning, and virtually every craft.")

Name: SodaAsh01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SodaAsh01_Description", "Sodium carbonate collected from dried lake beds or burned seaweed. Soda ash dramatically lowers the melting point of silica, making glass-making possible at achievable temperatures. This flux was essential to early glass production.")

Name: MineralGlaze01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "MineralGlaze01_Description", "Mineral compounds for pottery glazing. Early glazes were often accidental - ash falling on pottery in kilns created the first glazed surfaces. Later, potters learned to apply specific minerals to create colored, waterproof coatings.")

Name: CrudeChopper01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CrudeChopper01_Description", "A cobble with one end roughly flaked to create a chopping edge. This Oldowan-style tool represents humanitys first deliberate manufacture - technology over a million years old.")

Name: StoneScraper01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "StoneScraper01_Description", "A flake retouched along one edge to create a sturdy scraping surface. Essential for hide processing and woodworking.")

Name: FlintFlake01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FlintFlake01_Description", "A razor-sharp flake struck from a flint nodule. The edge can slice through hide and flesh with surgical precision.")

Name: RawHide01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "RawHide01_Description", "A fresh animal hide that must be processed quickly before it rots. The clock is ticking from the moment of skinning.")

Name: TannedLeather01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "TannedLeather01_Description", "Properly processed leather that resists rot and remains supple. The result of laborious treatment with brains or bark tannins.")

Name: Stick02
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Stick02_Description", "A branch with the bark removed, revealing smooth wood beneath.")

Name: FireDrill01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FireDrill01_Description", "A matched spindle and fireboard for creating fire through friction. Mastering this technique was one of humanitys greatest achievements.")

Name: BowDrill01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BowDrill01_Description", "A bow-driven fire-starting kit with spindle, fireboard, and bearing block. More efficient than hand-drilling.")

Name: FlintSpear01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FlintSpear01_Description", "A wooden shaft with a hafted flint point, bound with sinew and sealed with resin. The flint tip penetrates far deeper than wood.")

Name: FlintArrow01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FlintArrow01_Description", "An arrow with flint point and feather fletching. Mass-produced for hunting and warfare.")

Name: FishSpear01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "FishSpear01_Description", "A multi-pronged spear designed for fishing. The spread of points compensates for light refraction in water.")

Name: PolishedAxe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "PolishedAxe01_Description", "A ground and polished axe head of dense greenstone. Hours of grinding produced a tool that cuts faster and lasts longer than flaked stone.")

Name: DeadfallTrap01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DeadfallTrap01_Description", "A triggered trap that drops a heavy weight on prey. Set it and let it hunt while you sleep.")

Name: Snare01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Snare01_Description", "A noose trap that tightens when triggered. Catches small game with minimal effort.")

Name: StoneHoe01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "StoneHoe01_Description", "A flat stone blade hafted to a handle for breaking and tilling soil.")

Name: StoneSickle01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "StoneSickle01_Description", "A curved wooden handle set with sharp microliths for harvesting grain.")

Name: DropSpindle01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "DropSpindle01_Description", "A weighted spindle for spinning fiber into thread. The whorl provides momentum for continuous spinning.")

Name: CopperIngot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CopperIngot01_Description", "A bar of smelted copper, ready for casting or hammering into tools. The first true metal worked by humanity.")

Name: TinIngot01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "TinIngot01_Description", "A bar of smelted tin. Useless alone, but when alloyed with copper it creates bronze - harder than either.")

Name: BronzeSpear01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "BronzeSpear01_Description", "A spear with a socketed bronze head. The metal point is more durable and penetrating than stone.")

Name: RawGlass01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "RawGlass01_Description", "Fused silica - a miraculous transformation of sand into a transparent solid. Can be shaped while hot.")

Name: IronSpear01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronSpear01_Description", "A spear with a forged iron head. Superior to bronze in edge retention and impact strength.")

Name: IronArrowhead01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronArrowhead01_Description", "A small forged iron point for arrows. Mass-produced for warfare.")

Name: IronArrow01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronArrow01_Description", "An arrow with iron point and feather fletching. The iron tip punches through armor.")

Name: SmithTongs01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "SmithTongs01_Description", "Iron tongs for gripping hot metal. Essential for forge work.")

Name: IronAnvil01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "IronAnvil01_Description", "A heavy iron block for hammering metal. The foundation of any serious smithy.")

Name: Log01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Log01_Description", "A hefty section of tree trunk. Logs are the primary product of felling trees and serve as the foundation for construction, fuel, and further processing into planks and other wood products. The weight makes transport challenging but the utility is immense.")

Name: CopperNugget01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "CopperNugget01_Description", "A small piece of naturally occurring metallic copper. Native copper was the first metal worked by humans, simply hammered into shape without smelting. These rare surface finds sparked humanity's metallurgical journey over 10,000 years ago.")

Name: Tinder01
Description: NSLOCTEXT("DT_Items", "Tinder01_Description", "A bundle of extremely dry, fine material that catches fire from the smallest spark. Good tinder is the foundation of successful firemaking - dried bark, grass, seed fluff, or fungus that has been carefully prepared and kept bone-dry.")
